pedagogy.summary:
• Age/Topic: 7–8 (UK Y2→Y3, US Grade 2). Counting within 1,000, including skip-counting by 5s, 10s and 100s and understanding what changes as you cross into the hundreds.
• Standards — UK (DfE NC Mathematics): Y2 'count in steps of 2, 3, and 5 from 0, and in tens from any number' and use of <, >, =; Y3 'count from 0 in multiples of 4, 8, 50 and 100' and 'find 10 or 100 more or less than a given number', with fluent order and place value to 1,000.
• Standards — US (CCSS-M): 2.NBT.2 'Count within 1000; skip-count by 5s, 10s, and 100s'; 2.NBT.8 'mentally add/subtract 10 or 100 to a given number 100–900'.
• Operational details: the leap from within-100 to within-1000 is a PLACE-VALUE leap, not just a longer chant — +10 rolls the tens digit, +100 rolls the hundreds digit, and the child must see WHICH digit changes. Skip from non-round starts (e.g. 5s from 315, 100s from 240). The reliable stall is crossing hundred boundaries (190→200, 995→1000) where a digit carries.
• Checkpoint: skip-count aloud and predict the crossing. Tier A (7): count on in 10s and 100s from a round number within 1000 with a hundred-square/number-line prop. Tier B (7–8): skip-count by 5s/10s/100s from any start and state 10-more/100-more without counting. Tier C (8): cross 190→200 and 970→1000 explaining which digit rolls and why.
bestPractices: Frame within-1000 counting as PLACE VALUE in motion: use base-ten materials (hundreds flats, tens rods, unit cubes) so +10 physically adds a rod and +100 adds a flat — the child sees the digit that changes rather than reciting.

Make crossing a hundred boundary the explicit teaching event: pause at 190, ask 'what comes next in 10s?', and show the ten tens rods trading for one hundred flat so the roll from 190→200 is felt, not mysterious.
Skip-count from non-round and 'ragged' starts (5s from 315, 10s from 268, 100s from 240) so the pattern is a rule about which digit moves, not a memorised round-number chant.

Sync three representations of the same skip count — hundred/thousand grid highlights, equal jumps on a number line, and equal groups of counters — so 100s counting is seen as repeated equal groups (the multiplication/place-value bridge).
Separate '10 more' from 'count on ten by ones': ask for 10-more and 100-more instantly and check the child is rolling a digit, not counting 1,2,3… to prove the place-value idea has landed.
keyRepresentations: Scalable number line marked to 1,000 with equal jumps (jumps of 10 and of 100) to show constant step size and boundary crossings
Thousand grid / linked hundred squares where each skip count lights a column or diagonal, exposing the 5s, 10s and 100s patterns
Base-ten blocks (unit cubes, tens rods, hundreds flats) with regrouping — ten rods trade for one flat at the hundred boundary
Place-value columns (H T U) with digit-rollers so a step by 10 or 100 visibly advances one column and carries into the next
commonMisconceptions: Hundred-boundary stall — reaching 190 the child says '191, 192…' or '100-ten', not knowing 200 comes next; the decade/hundred bridge is the classic breakdown point.
'+10 means add a zero' / '+100 means add two zeros' — over-generalised from round numbers, so 268+10 becomes 2680 or 26810.
Treating the count as a longer rote chant and losing track of which digit changes, so skip-counting from a non-round start collapses.
Confusing tens and hundreds steps (counting 240, 250, 260 when asked to skip in 100s) because the difference between which column moves is not yet secure.
Losing the ones digit when skip-counting by 10s or 100s from a ragged start (315→320 instead of 325) because the child re-rounds to a decade.

learn.summary: For ages 7–8 (UK Y2→Y3, US Grade 2), skip-counting within 1,000 by 5s, 10s and 100s is a place-value event, not a longer chant: the learner must see WHICH digit rolls when adding 5, 10 or 100, and why a carry happens when crossing a hundred (190→200) or thousand (995→1000) boundary. Core activities drive a live place-value counter from round and ragged starts, with static reference and checking tasks as supports. Non-round starts (5s from 315, 100s from 150/240, 10s from 268) are emphasised so the learner holds the other digits fixed rather than re-rounding to a decade.

activities.title: Place-value skip-count playground (drive the carry)
feedback: If the learner predicts '2680' for 268+10 (the 'add a zero' error), pause the counter and show only the tens column advancing 6→7 to give 278; name that +10 moves one column, it does not append a digit.
If a ragged start collapses to a decade when counting on in 10s (315→320 instead of the correct 325), highlight the fixed ones digit (5) and replay the jump so the learner sees the ones stay put.
At the boundary, if the learner hesitates, show the ten tens-rods snapping into one hundred-flat so the carry is seen rather than recited.

When a '10 more' answer is produced instantly and correctly, confirm by rolling the tens digit (plus the regrouped next digit if a boundary is crossed), reinforcing that this is a place-value move, not counting on by ones.
activities.rationale: The classic stall is at hundred/thousand boundaries and from non-round starts; a learner-driven counter that synchronises grid, number line and place-value columns lets the child predict then see the exact digit that rolls, targeting the 'add a zero' and re-rounding misconceptions directly.
sourceClaims: 2.NBT.2: Count within 1000; skip-count by 5s, 10s, and 100s. 2.NBT.8: mentally add 10 or 100 to, and subtract 10 or 100 from, a given number 100–900.
Skip counting is a bridge to multiplicative reasoning and place value, not rote chanting; regrouping at ten/hundred boundaries is a core mastery checkpoint.
learnerActions: Set a start number — round (e.g. 240) or ragged (e.g. 315, 268) — and choose a step of +5, +10 or +100.
Before tapping, predict aloud the next number and say which digit you think will change.

Tap the step and watch three linked views move together: a thousand grid lights the landed number, a number line draws one equal jump, and place-value columns (H-T-U, with a Th column that appears when you reach 1000) roll the digit or digits that change.
Stop deliberately at 190 and predict 'what comes next in 10s?', then tap +10 and watch ten tens-rods trade for one hundred-flat while the hundreds digit rolls 1→2 and the tens resets to 0.
Repeat the boundary move by counting in 5s up to 995→1000 and describe, in your own words, which columns carried.

Switch to a '10 more / 100 more instantly' challenge: state the answer without counting on by ones, then tap to check which digit rolled (just one digit unless the step crosses a hundred or thousand boundary, e.g. 195 → 205).
activities.intendedInsight: Adding 10 rolls the tens digit and adding 100 rolls the hundreds digit; if no boundary is crossed, the other digits stay the same. When a hundred/thousand boundary is crossed (e.g. 190 → 200), the next place up also changes because of regrouping (ten of one place trading for one of the next), not a mysterious jump.

activities.title: Hands-on regrouping with base-ten materials
feedback: If the learner counts 150, 250, 350 but drops the 50 to say 100, 200, 300, point to the five tens rods still sitting on the mat and ask what should have stayed the same.
If the learner recites a number but adds the wrong piece, map the spoken digit to the matching column of blocks before continuing.
activities.rationale: Base-ten materials make +10/+100 a concrete regrouping action, so the child can see which digit changes rather than reciting a longer chant; this grounds the live on-screen counter.
sourceClaims: Skip counting is a bridge to multiplicative reasoning and place value, not rote chanting; regrouping at ten/hundred boundaries is a core mastery checkpoint.
learnerActions: Build a start number with hundreds flats, tens rods and unit cubes (e.g. 190 as one flat and nine rods).
To add 10, physically add one tens rod; to add 100, add one hundreds flat — and say which digit changed.
At 190, add the tenth rod, then trade ten rods for one hundreds flat to make 200, and say 'the tens rolled to 0 and the hundreds went up by one'.
Skip-count by 100s from 150 using flats, keeping the five tens and nothing in the ones fixed, to reach 250, 350 … 950.
activities.intendedInsight: Adding 10 or 100 physically adds a rod or a flat, and crossing a boundary is the concrete act of trading ten rods for one flat — making the digit that changes something the learner can handle and see, not just recite.

activities.title: Annotated thousand-square and place-value reference
feedback: If the learner names the wrong column for a step, point back to the lit pattern and the H-T-U labels so the step size maps to a single column.
Use the boundary flap as a reminder that the join between 190 and 200 is a trade, to be practised live with the counter or blocks.
activities.rationale: A static annotated reference is a strong support for recognising patterns and naming columns, but recognition alone does not enact the carry or recompute from a ragged start, so it accompanies rather than replaces the manipulable counter.
learnerActions: Study a thousand grid / linked hundred squares where a 10s count lights one column, a 5s count lights two columns, and a 100s count lights the same position in each hundred square, and name the pattern you see.
Tap a highlighted 100s column to reveal the note 'each step adds one hundred — the hundreds digit changes', and name the H, T, U columns.
Open the flap at the 190→200 join to read how ten tens trade for one hundred.
activities.intendedInsight: The 5s/10s/100s patterns fall in predictable places (columns for 5s and 10s, the same position in each hundred square for 100s), and naming the place-value columns helps the learner say which digit each step advances.

activities.title: Checking and diagnostic skip-count tasks
feedback: Expected: 150, 250 … 950; 480, 485 … 520 crossing 500 correctly; 1000, 990, 980 …; and 620, 720, 820, 920, 1020 crossing the thousand boundary cleanly. (985, __, 1005 fills to 995.)
'10 more than 268' = 278; if a learner offers 2680, that is the 'add a zero' error — show the tens digit rolling 6→7 instead. ('100 more than 613' = 713.)
If the learner snaps 100s-from-150 to 100, 200, 300, name the dropped 50 and re-run keeping tens and ones fixed.

If an error appears precisely at 495→500 or at 1000 while mid-run counting is fine, treat it as a boundary-bridge gap: rehearse just 490, 495, 500, 505 and 980, 990, 1000, 1010 on a number line, naming the regrouping — do not re-drill the whole sequence.
If backward counting breaks only at boundaries, practise short backward runs across each boundary as its own skill; do not assume backward fluency arrives with forward.
activities.rationale: Boundary-crossing and ragged-start items probe the key misconceptions crisply and separate secure three-digit place value from a learner who snaps to pure multiples or re-rounds; placed after the constructive activities they primarily verify the insight, while their feedback can reteach when an error appears.
sourceClaims: 2.NBT.2: Count within 1000; skip-count by 5s, 10s, and 100s. 2.NBT.8: mentally add 10 or 100 to, and subtract 10 or 100 from, a given number 100–900.
Skip counting is a bridge to multiplicative reasoning and place value, not rote chanting; regrouping at ten/hundred boundaries is a core mastery checkpoint.
learnerActions: Order a set of 100s cards from 240 and fill blanks in sequences that cross a boundary, e.g. 985, __, 1005.
Answer '100 more than 613' and '10 more than 268', writing the single digit that changed.
Count on in 100s from 150 up to 950; count in 5s from 480 up to 520; count back in 10s from 1000; count on in 100s from 620 and say what happens when the count passes 1000 (920 → 1020).
Explain for each: which digit changed and which stayed the same.
activities.intendedInsight: Fluency means changing only the relevant place and crossing hundred and thousand boundaries cleanly, from non-round starts and in both directions.

activities.title: Count-with-me partner rehearsal (spoken practice)
feedback: If the learner supplies a wrong boundary number, pause and return to a number line or blocks to show the regrouping before resuming the count.
Reward a correct boundary supply by having the learner name the digit that changed.
activities.rationale: Spoken turn-taking rehearses the sequence orally and prompts boundary crossings; it adds oral practice alongside the visual/place-value work rather than replacing the manipulable or concrete activities.
learnerActions: Take turns skip-counting aloud with a counting buddy, alternating each number in a 10s or 100s run.
When the buddy hesitates at 190 in a 10s run, supply the next number (200) and say which digits rolled.
Say each number clearly and, at boundaries, state what carried before moving on.
activities.intendedInsight: Rehearsing the count aloud, especially at the deliberate hesitation at a boundary, builds oral fluency and the habit of naming the carry.

constraints: The annotated thousand-square and place-value reference is a scaffold: it shows patterns and names columns but does not itself enact the carry or recompute from a ragged start, so pair it with a manipulable counter or base-ten materials.

Checking/diagnostic tasks are primarily for verifying the pattern and catching misconceptions; their feedback can also prompt reteaching, but they are best placed after the constructive activities rather than being the sole means of building the place-value insight.
Spoken partner practice rehearses the sequence orally but does not by itself make the digit-rolling visible; keep it alongside visual/concrete work.

Base-ten cutouts and rods are physical approximations of the ideal place-value idea: use the trade of ten rods for one flat to represent regrouping, and connect the concrete piece to the spoken digit and the written column.
Practise backward counting across boundaries as its own skill rather than assuming it transfers automatically from forward fluency.
When crossing a boundary during a ragged-start count, keep the ones/tens that should stay fixed in view so the learner does not re-round to a decade.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched and the activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

The legacy row claims a talking character 'adds little the manipulative doesn't do better' and that a 3D scene 'adds spatial overhead with no conceptual payoff'; these comparative-efficacy/necessity claims are not established by the cited sources, so the conversation activity is retained as optional spoken practice and the 3D option is omitted rather than asserting it has no value.

The legacy 'strong' quiz note says it 'verifies rather than builds' the insight; this has been scoped to a placement limit (checking tasks follow constructive work; their feedback can still reteach), not retained as a universal claim that such tasks cannot teach.
One source (CCSS-M 2.NBT) is marked verified:false and the NCETM claim is unverified; confidence should not be upgraded on that basis.

Diagnostic answer sequences and expected errors (150→250…950; 480→520 crossing 500; 620→1020 crossing 1000; blank 995 in 985,__,1005; 2680 as the add-a-zero error; 268+10=278; 613+100=713) were checked for arithmetic consistency and carried through to learner-facing feedback.

The original misconception example '315→320 instead of 325' is only an error when counting on in 10s (315+10=325); 315→320 is correct under a +5 step, so the step is named explicitly in the feedback to avoid ambiguity.

probeDeeper: What digit changes when you count in 100s from 150? What stays the same?
assess.correctAnswer: 150, 250, …, 950; 480, 485, …, 520 (crossing 500 correctly); 1000, 990, 980…; and 620, 720, 820, 920, 1020 — changing only the relevant place and crossing the thousand boundary cleanly.

errorPatterns.pattern: snaps to pure multiples — counting in 100s from 150 drops the 50 and gives 100, 200, 300
errorPatterns.nextMove: use a place-value chart or bead string so only the hundreds digit ticks while the 50 stays fixed; name what stays and what changes
errorPatterns.revealedBy: loses the tens/ones and recites round hundreds

errorPatterns.pattern: hundred/thousand boundary break — 5s or 10s stall or err when crossing 500 or 1000 (e.g. 495→'400', or can't pass 1000)
errorPatterns.nextMove: do NOT re-drill the whole sequence — rehearse just the bridges (490, 495, 500, 505; 980, 990, 1000, 1010) on a number line, naming the regrouping
errorPatterns.revealedBy: an error precisely at the boundary while mid-run counting is fine

errorPatterns.pattern: backward collapse over boundaries — counts back in 10s fine until a hundred or the thousand, then errs
errorPatterns.nextMove: do NOT expect backward to arrive with forward — practise short backward runs across each boundary on a number line as its own skill
errorPatterns.revealedBy: backward errors that appear only at boundaries

responseLevels.gap: Reverts to pure multiples (100, 200…) instead of keeping the other digits; breaks down at hundred/thousand boundaries.
responseLevels.full: Counts within 1000 by 5s/10s/100s forwards and backwards from any start, changing only the relevant place and crossing hundred and thousand boundaries cleanly.
responseLevels.partial: Skip-counts within 1000 from standard starts but falters counting from a non-multiple, or when crossing 500/1000, or backwards.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Count on in 100s starting from 150: 150, 250, 350… up to 950. Now count in 5s from 480 up to 520. Then count backwards in 10s from 1000 for a bit. Last, count on by 100s from 620 — what happens at 1000? (Watch counting in 100s from a non-multiple, crossing 500 in 5s, and crossing 1000.)
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: Counting in 100s from 150 (a non-multiple of 100) tests holding tens and ones constant while moving hundreds; the 5s run 480→520 tests crossing a hundred boundary; going through 1000 tests the thousand boundary. A child with three-digit place value handles all; a weaker child snaps 100s-from-150 to 100, 200, 300, mis-crosses 495→500, or stalls at 1000.
